value.body: A reservoir engineer works out how much oil or gas a field holds and how to get it out — where to drill, how fast to produce, and when to use methods such as water injection. Upstream oil and gas companies and consultancies hire them. Most days are office-based: analysing production and pressure data, running simulation models and working with geologists and production engineers.

items.label: Typical entry
items.value: B.Tech in Petroleum; an M.Tech or MS is common

items.label: Common tools
items.value: Reservoir simulators, Petrel-type modelling, Excel, Python

items.label: Work pattern
items.value: Mostly office-based, with occasional field visits

value.title: How you get in
value.body: A few freshers join upstream companies directly as reservoir trainees, through GATE-based PSU recruitment or campus hiring. Many enter after an M.Tech or MS, or move in from field production roles after a few years.

value.title: At a glance
items: Entry openings are fewer than for field roles.
Common next roles: senior reservoir engineer, field development planning, asset management.
Simulation and data skills carry over to some energy-transition work such as carbon storage.
